```text
Peak Poker Performance

daunting, but if followed would almost certainly lead most of us into a
much higher echelon of success. This idea of being slightly obsessed and
willing to go the extra mile is a keystone practice of peak poker perform-
ers as well as of those who achieve long-term success in other disciplines,
but it is a very difficult ideal to achieve. There are so many possibilities
that compete for our attention that making a true defining commitment
to any one endeavor feels like we are closing off equally attractive op-
tions, and there lies the conundrum. If you truly want to attain peak per-
formance, you have to be willing to make a definitive commitment for the
long haul.
    I recently read a fantastic book by Gary Keller and Jay Papasan called
The One Thing where they maintain that if you want the best chance to
succeed at anything, you have to be super focused on your one thing.
They reiterate the idea that it is impossible to dabble in a number of areas
if you want to attain true excellence, and call this ideology “going small.”
They argue very convincingly that if you want to achieve massive success
then you have to put all of your energy into your one thing.
    It may seem strange that these authors advocate going small when
what you are after are big results. Such is the paradox that was originally
discovered by the Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto in the late 1800s.
Better known as the Pareto principle, he determined that 20% of our ac-
tions determine 80% of our results. Typically, we put too much emphasis
on things that simply don’t matter. Keller and Papasan transform this
principle into their concept of “going small” and advise that we should ig-
nore all the things we could do and only focus on those we should do to
get the results we desire. They say that by making our focus extremely
narrow, we can achieve extraordinary results.
    If you look at the annals of peak poker performers you’ll see that the
real driver of success is how big a commitment is made to the truly im-
portant activities. Time is a commodity and one that peak performers
know they have to manage diligently. In his book The 80/20 Principle
Robert Koch sums up this idea by saying, “The 80/20 principle asserts
that a minority of causes, inputs or effort usually lead to a majority of re-
```

```text
                                                         What’s Your Why?

sults, outputs or rewards” (2011). For all practical purposes this means
that some of your efforts are more valuable than others. Keller and Pa-
pasan argue very persuasively that success comes to those who focus on
the “vital few” as opposed to the “trivial many.” The secret is that you
must focus on building your success slowly, patiently, and diligently over
time by taking action on the things that will reap you the greatest re-
wards. There are no shortcuts, as much as we all wish there were, and
peak poker performers have figured this out.
   Keller and Papasan are certainly not the only persons to advocate tak-
ing committed, focused action. Gary Cardone posed a similar idea in his
2011 book The 10X Rule, in which he made the compelling case that if
you want to be truly successful in any endeavor, you must set perform-
ance targets that are 10 times what you think you want and then do 10
times what you think it will take to reach those targets. He argued that
most people are simply not willing to put in this much effort, which he
calls “pure domination mentality.” As he describes it, people with this
mentality aren’t really attempting to achieve their goal; rather they are
looking to dominate an entire sector.
   How about you? What area of poker (or your life, for that matter) are
you interested in dominating? Do you have a clear picture of what suc-
cess looks like for you? Creating a compelling vision is really the first step
in peak performance. The only way to be “all-in” is to have a clear vision
of where you want to finish. It helps to have a clear idea of why you want
to achieve poker success. Here are a few questions that you should an-
swer to help you understand your vision:

   ♠ Why did you choose to start playing poker?
   ♠ Why are you still playing the game?
   ♠ Why do you want to be great at it?
   ♠ What do you really want to achieve in the game (or from the
       game)?
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

  To delve deeper with this idea, consider the steps that Todd Henry
(2015) outlined as imperative to peak performance and mastery:

     ♠ Articulate an identity of who we are (or who we would like to
        become).
     ♠ Create an ideal vision of where we want to go.
     ♠ Develop a map or path to mastery, which we follow diligently.

   In three simple steps, you have a clear formula for mastery – which we
will unpack more fully as we go through the book. They seem so simple on
the surface, but if we go deeper, it’s possible to see how truly difficult it is
to achieve mastery in any endeavor. How many good poker players do
you know who have not fully realized their potential? Maybe you even
see yourself in this category: you know you have room for growth and
improvement, but something holds you back. Maybe you have become
frustrated while waiting for a major breakthrough to happen, and perhaps
you have even considered quitting or severely curtailing your play. Most
players start the game with high aspirations and are strongly motivated to
work at learning the game, but then something happens and they flame
out. Having a strong commitment is one thing, but putting the time and
effort in (often with no results to show for it) is quite another. Sadly,
many people give up when they are just short of a breakthrough!
   Consider this. A certain amount of activation energy is required to
start a chemical reaction. According to Michael Lardon (2008), paper
burns at 451 degrees Fahrenheit – not 450 degrees, but exactly at 451.
You may be putting your heart and effort into rubbing two sticks to-
gether to make a fire out of some paper and leaves, but if you give up at
450 degrees – just 1 degree off the target, you’ll be stuck with a whole
bunch of wasted effort. If you had stuck with it just a little bit longer a
chain reaction of warm goodness would have occurred. The moral of the
story is to make sure you don’t give up too soon on your poker efforts!
You could be closer to success than you realize.
```

```text
                                                       What’s Your Why?

    Great players know that they have to push a little more and prepare a
little better than their opponents if they want to achieve all that they are
capable of over the long haul. The difference between good and great has
been shown to be quite small across a wide range of disciplines, and Jona-
than Little remarked to me recently that the best players are not that
much better than the almost best players! Sometimes, all it takes to get
to the next level is just a little bit more work. We know from countless
research studies on the development of talent that the road to success is
paved with patient, diligent, consistent action.
    The first step in maintaining performance at a high level is a commit-
ment to a vision of yourself as great poker player. Abraham Maslow, one
of the greatest humanistic thinkers of all time, believed that we all pos-
sess an innate striving towards mastery and that our striving needs to be
substantive and meaningful, otherwise we will feel dissatisfied. Poker is an
interesting game because there is a great deal of emphasis put on money,
but money is not everything. In fact, if you only focus on the monetary
aspects of the game, you are likely to feel a sense of meaninglessness as
your length of time in the game increases. Being committed to the goal of
making a ton of money just for the sake of making it is not a recipe for
happiness, contrary to what many believe. Rather, it is critical to have
some sort of deeper “why” for your pursuits.
    There are many reasons that might underpin your wish for success, in-
cluding:

   ♠ thriving on excitement and competition
   ♠ liking that the game is always evolving and thus always presenting
       new and different challenges
   ♠ enjoying the satisfaction of playing well and solving problems with
       limited information
   ♠ having a passion for the game (or games in general)
   ♠ relishing the thrill of victory.
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

   Take some time to consider your “why” for playing poker. Why is mas-
tering poker meaningful to you? What sorts of things could you do with
money and notoriety that you are not able to do now? Perhaps you have
a dream of providing for your family or of doing charity work. These are
noble ideals which can enhance your sense of identity as a poker player.
Having a strong sense of purpose for your mastery of poker helps mani-
fest a compelling vision, which heightens motivation for putting in the
necessary work. It is only through such an impactful vision that you can
develop a solid foundation of commitment.
   I would like to take a minute to point out one caveat regarding mas-
tery. It is a personal journey. Even though you can look to other players
and coaches for guidance and support, it is imperative that you run your
own race. By this I mean that each one of us has unique skills, experi-
ences, and opportunities that will make our path somewhat different
from everyone else’s. There is no point in comparing your progress to an-
other’s. If you allow thoughts of envy, spite, or ego into your conscious-
ness, you can easily find yourself derailed. Instead, make a commitment to
work your plan. Figure out what your road to mastery is and set about
doing it. As Sonja Lyubomirsky (2008) notes, it is not possible to be
happy and envious at the same time. If you are comparing yourself to
other players, a process known as social comparison, you’ll find yourself
feeling chronically insecure. If you want to be happier with what you are
doing, stop comparing yourself to others.

Growth Mindset
Carol Dweck is the leading researcher in the area of mindset and she
takes up where Maslow left off. Her years of study have led her to con-
clude that the view you adopt for yourself profoundly affects your life. It
is a simple mindset that can determine if you achieve as much as you
want to achieve and if you live the kind of life you want to lead. If you
want to achieve a great deal, you need to adopt what she calls a growth
mindset. If you believe that you can cultivate your talents through your
efforts, you have a growth mindset. Contrast this with a fixed mindset,
```

```text
                                                           What’s Your Why?

which is the belief that our traits and abilities are set in stone. Obviously,
if you think your talents, traits, and abilities are fixed, you are not likely to
be too committed to changing them. On the other hand, if you think that
application and experience can shape and mold you, you’ll be a lot more
likely to be committed to trying to change.
    As Dweck eloquently puts it, “a person’s true potential is unknown and
unknowable; that is it is impossible to foresee what can be accomplished
with years of passion, toil, and training” (2006). If you are blessed with
this type of mindset, you’ll approach failure as a learning experience,
whereas if you are cursed with a fixed mindset, you’ll see failure as a sign
that you are not smart and not talented. It’s not too difficult to figure out
which mindset is beneficial to the peak performance mindset.
    As an aside, mindset is a belief and beliefs are totally changeable. All
you have to do is be willing to see yourself as someone who can put in the
effort and who is able to learn, grow, and change. Change your mindset,
commit to putting in the work, and get after it. Dweck also makes a
strong case that our society loves to focus on “natural” talent and people
who are “born” geniuses. She cites case after case that proves this idea is
just not true. For example, the great golfer Ben Hogan was extremely un-
coordinated as a child! She points out that both Darwin and Tolstoy were
considered average, ordinary children. It was not until much later that
their “genius” was uncovered.
    If it’s one thing I want this chapter to hammer home, it’s that we can
reach our highest potential if only we take action. Intentional effort and
consistent progress are the true keys to a pure domination mentality.

A Word on Mediocrity
Mediocrity is the kiss of death for peak performance. The word comes
from the Latin words medius meaning middle, and ocris, which means
rugged mountain. Mediocrity literally means being stuck in the middle of a
rugged mountain! If you take one summit as your ability and potential and
```
